title: Faith the best wealth
hookLine: a fierce spirit orders the Buddha in and out, then threatens him with a riddle

cards: Get out. So the Buddha gets up and goes out. Come in.
So he comes back in. Get out. He goes.
Come in. He comes. The spirit is a yakkha named Alavaka, and this is his house, and he's testing how far he can push this calm visitor.
The fourth time he says get out, the Buddha says: no, friend, I won't. Do what you have to do. And Alavaka makes his threat.

teach.h: THREE TIMES YES, THE FOURTH TIME NO
NO ONE CAN SPLIT MY HEART
teach.b: In all the world, he says, I see no one who could scramble my mind or split my heart. But ask whatever you like. Notice what he did first.
Three times, he went along. Not out of fear, the commentary says, but to soften a hard mind with gentleness. Only the fourth time, when obeying would have been just a game, did he say no.
Then the questions come, in verse.
What is the best wealth a person has? Faith, the Buddha answers, saddha, trust in what is good. What, practiced well, brings happiness?
The teaching. What is the sweetest of all tastes? Truth.
Living how is the best life? Living with wisdom. Then the deeper ones.
How does one cross the flood?
By faith. How does one cross the sea? By care, by not being careless.
How does one get past suffering? By effort. How does one become pure?
By wisdom. Why faith? One way to hear it: look at what the threat was.
Alavaka could take your mind, your body, your life. But trust in something good is a wealth that's still yours while you're being threatened. It's what lets you answer calmly.

At the end, the fierce spirit says, in words close to yesterday's spirits, that he'll travel from village to village, honoring the one who is fully awake. Theravada chants still recall the taming of Alavaka.

how: The taming of Alavaka is one of the episodes recalled in the Jayamangala Gatha, a verse chant of the Buddha's victories recited in Theravada temples and homes.

o: a large store of gold and grain
trust in what is good, the best wealth
a fortune won in a contest of riddles

s: the Buddha refuses Alavaka's very first order
he goes out and comes in three times, and only refuses the fourth.
Alavaka threatens to throw him across the Ganges
if he can't answer the riddles: or scramble his mind, or split his heart.
the Buddha says truth is the sweetest of tastes
and faith is a person's best wealth.

games.q: you're the Buddha. for the fourth time, the spirit orders you out of his house. what do you do?
o: leave again, to keep the peace.
say no, calmly: do what you must.
games.why: he went along three times to soften a hard mind; the fourth time he declined calmly, and the questions began.

practice: Picture a small threat arriving, a demanding message, a tense meeting, a sharp relative, and notice any jolt in the chest.

Breathe out slowly and picture yourself answering the way the Buddha did, not shrinking, not striking back: ask what they want, and answer plainly. Let your shoulders drop, and notice what's still yours.

wordCard.voice: saddha. The Buddha's first answer to the threatening spirit Alavaka: trust in what is good is a person's best wealth. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Alavaka: the spirit of Alavi, named for the town where the story is set.

carryVoice: Your line: answer once, calmly and plainly. Some wealth stays yours, even under threat. Day five hundred eighty-seven, done.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 1.10, Alavaka Sutta (also Samyutta Nikaya 10.12)
Commentary on Sn 1.10: why the Buddha complied three times
